course.description: One machine stops being enough long before you expect it: the table no longer fits in RAM, one disk can't take the writes, one primary is one outage. The fix is always the same sentence ("split the data across machines") and the hard part is always the same three questions: *which machine owns this key*, *what happens when machines come and go*, and *how do machines that never talk to each other hand out unique names*. lessons.title: Partitioning and IDs
lessons.explanation:
# 11 · Partitioning and IDs

One machine stops being enough long before you expect it: the table no
longer fits in RAM, one disk can't take the writes, one primary is one
outage. The fix is always the same sentence ("split the data across
machines") and the hard part is always the same three questions: *which
machine owns this key*, *what happens when machines come and go*, and
*how do machines that never talk to each other hand out unique names*.
This module answers them with the small, exact algorithms that real
databases, caches and CDNs run: modulo sharding, range partitions, the
consistent-hash ring, rendezvous hashing, Snowflake ids, base62 codes,
Bloom filters and quorum replication.

## The mental model

### 1 · Partitioning is a function from key to owner

Every scheme in this module is a pure function `owner(key, cluster)`.
What separates them is what the function preserves and what it costs
when the cluster changes:

| scheme | owner(key) | range scans | keys moved when N → N+1 | seen in |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| hash mod N | `floorMod(hash(key), N)` | no | about N/(N+1): almost all | hand-rolled app sharding, early memcached clients |
| range | how many split points ≤ key | **yes** | only the range being split | Bigtable, HBase, CockroachDB, Spanner |
| consistent ring | first point clockwise of `hash(key)` | no | about 1/(N+1), all to the new node | Dynamo, Cassandra, Riak, ketama |
| rendezvous (HRW) | node with the highest `hash(node, key)` | no | about 1/(N+1), all to the new node | Apache Ignite, Tahoe-LAFS |

```java
Math.floorMod(key.hashCode(), shards)                 // never % on a hash
var hit = ring.ceilingEntry(hash(key));               // first point >= h
(hit != null ? hit : ring.firstEntry()).getValue();   // ... or wrap
nodes.stream().min(byScoreDescThenName(key))          // rendezvous
```

### 2 · Count the keys that move

Rebalancing cost is the number to put on the whiteboard. With mod-N a
key stays put only when `h mod N == h mod (N+1)`, so growing 4 → 5
shards moves about 80% of the data (exercise 01 measures 814 of 1000).
That is 80% of the rows copied over the network and 80% of the cache
entries suddenly missing, all at once. Consistent and rendezvous
hashing move about 1/N, and every moved key goes to the node that
joined:

```
mod N, 4 → 5 shards            ring / HRW, 4 → 5 nodes
A B C D A B C D A B ...        A A B B C C D D ...
A B C D E A B C D E ...        A A B E C C D D ...   ← only E's arc moved
  ↑ almost every key moves
```

### 3 · Virtual nodes and tie-breaks make it fair and deterministic

A ring with one point per node has arcs of wildly different lengths;
one node can own half the keys. Give every node 100-256 points and the
arcs average out (exercise 04 checks the spread), and when a node
leaves, its load spreads over everyone instead of one neighbour.
Rendezvous hashing needs no virtual nodes, but its comparator must be
**total** (score, then name): two routers that list the nodes in a
different order must still agree on the owner.

### 4 · IDs without a coordinator

A central sequence is a single point of failure and a round trip per
insert. Snowflake packs everything a unique id needs into 64 bits:

```
 0 | 41 bits: ms since custom epoch | 10 bits: worker | 12 bits: sequence
       (about 69 years)               (1024 workers)    (4096 ids per ms)
```

Time in the high bits makes ids sort by creation time (friendly to
B-tree indexes); the worker id makes two machines' ids disjoint; the
sequence counts within one millisecond. Base62 is the presentation
layer: the same number written with `0-9a-zA-Z` is a short, URL-safe
code, and `capacity(7)` = 62^7 ≈ 3.5 trillion is the back-of-envelope
answer to "how long do short links need to be?". (Sequential ids give
guessable codes; real shorteners scramble the id first, for example by
multiplying by a large odd constant modulo 62^7.)

### 5 · Ask "maybe?" cheaply, and ask enough replicas

A **Bloom filter** is a bit array that answers *definitely not* or
*maybe*. LSM stores (LevelDB, RocksDB, Cassandra) keep one per file so
a lookup for a missing key skips nearly every disk read. Sizing is
arithmetic, not guesswork:

```
false-positive rate ≈ (1 - e^(-k·n/m))^k        best k = (m/n)·ln 2
10 bits per key  →  k = 7  →  about 0.8% false positives
```

**Quorums** decide how many of N copies a write and a read must touch.
If `R + W > N`, every read set overlaps every write set, so at least
one replica the read contacts has the latest version:

```
N=3, W=2, R=2      write lands on {0,1}   read asks {1,2}   overlap at 1 ✓
N=3, W=1, R=1      write lands on {0}     read asks {1}     no overlap ✗ stale
```

## The details that bite

1. **`%` keeps the sign.** `hashCode()` is negative half the time and
   `-3 % 10 == -3`. `Math.abs` is not the fix:
   `Math.abs(Integer.MIN_VALUE) < 0`, and `"polygenelubricants"`
   hashes to exactly that. Use `Math.floorMod` (exercises 01 and 07).
2. **A boundary key belongs to the range it starts.** With split point
   `"g"`, `partitionOf("g")` is 1, not 0. `Collections.binarySearch`
   returns the index of an exact hit, so the partition is `index + 1`.
3. **Scan ends are exclusive.** `[a, g)` touches only partition 0;
   counting partition 1 because `"g"` starts it makes every range query
   fan out one partition too far.
4. **`ceilingEntry`, not `higherEntry`, and wrap around.** A key whose
   hash equals a point belongs to that point; a key past the last point
   belongs to the first. Forgetting the wrap returns `null`.
5. **Comparators on hashes: `Long.compare`, never subtraction.**
   `(int) (a - b)` overflows for hashes near the ends of the long range
   and silently picks the wrong owner. Then break ties on the name.
6. **A full sequence must wait, not wrap or spill.** The 4097th id in
   one millisecond would either repeat sequence 0 (a duplicate) or carry
   into the worker bits (someone else's id). Wait for the clock to tick.
7. **Clocks go backwards.** NTP steps and VM pauses happen. Issuing ids
   from a rewound clock can repeat ids already handed out; refuse.
8. **Overflow is silent.** `long * 62` wraps, so a too-long base62 code
   decodes to a negative id. `Math.multiplyExact`/`addExact` throw.
9. **Integer division hides in formulas.** `bits / items` with ints is
   `6` for 10000/1500, and the optimal `k` comes out 4 instead of 5.
10. **"Highest version", not "first replica that answered".** Arrival
    order is not a timeline. Take the newest version among the replies,
    then read-repair the contacted replicas that are behind.

## Cheat table

| question | reach for |
| --- | --- |
| which shard, N fixed forever | `Math.floorMod(hash, N)` |
| range scans, ordered keys, splitting hot spots | sorted split points + binary search |
| nodes join and leave often | consistent ring (`TreeMap` + vnodes) or rendezvous |
| N replicas per key in a stable order | rendezvous: sort nodes by score, take the top N |
| unique, time-ordered ids with no coordinator | Snowflake bit packing |
| short public codes | base62 of an id |
| "is it definitely absent?" in a few bits per key | Bloom filter |
| "will my read see my write?" | is `R + W > N`? |

## How this connects

- **09-caching** puts a cache in front of one store. Sharding a cache
  tier with mod-N turns every resize into a mass of misses, which is
  why cache clients moved to consistent hashing.
- **10-rate-limits-and-resilience**: per-key limits and idempotency
  stores only work when every client computes the same owner for a key.
- **12-messaging-and-events**: Kafka assigns a message to a partition
  by hashing its key modulo the partition count. Ordering is per
  partition, so adding partitions to a live topic reshuffles keys and
  breaks per-key order, the exact cost exercise 01 measures.
- **13-storage-and-consistency**: quorums give overlap; vector clocks,
  LWW registers and CRDTs decide what "newest" means when versions
  conflict, and the LSM exercise is where Bloom filters earn their keep.

## Exercises

| # | file | ★ | what you build |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 01 | `01-hash-sharding.java` | ★☆☆ | `floorMod` sharding and the cost of changing N |
| 02 | `02-base62-codes.java` | ★☆☆ | URL-shortener codes with overflow-safe decoding |
| 03 | `03-range-partitions.java` | ★★☆ | sorted ranges, range scans, hot-range splits |
| 04 | `04-consistent-hash-ring.java` | ★★☆ | a hash ring with virtual nodes on a `TreeMap` |
| 05 | `05-rendezvous-hashing.java` | ★★☆ | highest-random-weight owners and replica lists |
| 06 | `06-snowflake-ids.java` | ★★☆ | 64-bit time-ordered ids with an injected clock |
| 07 | `07-bloom-filter.java` | ★★★ | a double-hashed Bloom filter and its sizing math |
| 08 | `08-quorum-replication.java` | ★★★ | N/R/W replication, stale reads and read repair |

Do the warm-ups and core in order. Stretch if time allows.

---

**Next:** `bootcamp/12-messaging-and-events`

javabootcamp/11-partitioning-and-ids/01-.instructions:
**Concepts:** sharding · hashCode · Math.floorMod · rebalancing cost  
**Level:** ★☆☆ warm-up

A user service has outgrown one database, so rows are split across N
shards by hashing the key. Write three static methods:
shardOf(key, shards) is the key's hashCode() modulo shards, always in
0..shards-1 (a hash of -3 with 10 shards is shard 7, never -3);
shards < 1 → IllegalArgumentException. distribute(keys, shards) maps
EVERY shard number 0..shards-1 to its keys in input order (an unused
shard maps to an empty list). movedKeys(keys, from, to) counts the keys
whose shard changes when the shard count goes from `from` to `to`.

    shardOf("a", 10)                     → 7      ("a".hashCode() is 97)
    shardOf("polygenelubricants", 10)    → 2      (hashCode is MIN_VALUE)
    distribute(["a", "b"], 3)            → {0=[], 1=[a], 2=[b]}
    movedKeys(1000 keys, 4, 5)           → most of them

hint: Math.abs(Integer.MIN_VALUE) is still negative.
javabootcamp/11-partitioning-and-ids/01-.explanation:
hash(key) mod N is the simplest partitioning there is: no lookup table,
any client can compute the owner, and keys spread as evenly as the hash
does. Memcached client libraries, early Redis sharding and countless
"user_id % 16" schemes work exactly like this.
The Java trap is the sign. hashCode() is any int, including negatives,
and Java's % keeps the sign of the dividend: -3 % 10 is -3, an index
that does not exist. Math.abs looks like the fix but is wrong twice:
it maps -3 to shard 3 (a different answer from every client that uses
floorMod), and Math.abs(Integer.MIN_VALUE) overflows back to
MIN_VALUE, so "polygenelubricants" would still land on shard -8.
Math.floorMod always returns 0..N-1.
The real lesson is movedKeys. Going from 4 to 5 shards moves about
4/5 of all keys, because a key stays put only when h mod 4 == h mod 5.
Doubling from 4 to 8 moves about half. Every moved key is a row to
copy and a cache entry to miss, which is why growing a mod-N cluster
is an outage-sized event, and why the next exercises (range
partitions, consistent hashing, rendezvous hashing) exist.
distribute pre-fills every shard so callers can iterate 0..N-1 without
null checks, and it keeps input order by appending as it walks.

javabootcamp/11-partitioning-and-ids/02-.instructions:
**Concepts:** base conversion · URL shorteners · overflow · Math.multiplyExact  
**Level:** ★☆☆ warm-up

A URL shortener stores each link under a numeric id and shows it as a
base62 code with the digits of ALPHABET (0-9, then a-z, then A-Z, so
'a' is 10 and 'A' is 36). encode(id) writes id >= 0 in base62 with no
leading zeros (0 is "0"); a negative id → IllegalArgumentException.
decode(code) reverses it (leading zeros allowed, case matters); an
empty code, a character outside ALPHABET, or a value too big for a long
→ IllegalArgumentException. capacity(length) is how many distinct codes
of exactly that many characters exist, counting leading zeros (62 to
the power length); length < 1 or a result that overflows a long →
IllegalArgumentException.

    encode(61)      → "Z"            encode(62)     → "10"
    decode("A")     → 36             decode("0a")   → 10
    encode(Long.MAX_VALUE)           → "aZl8N0y58M7"
    decode("aZl8N0y58M8")            → IllegalArgumentException
    capacity(7)     → 3521614606208  (3.5 trillion links)

hint: Math.multiplyExact and Math.addExact throw instead of wrapping.
javabootcamp/11-partitioning-and-ids/02-.explanation:
Base62 is ordinary base conversion with a 62-character digit set: take
id % 62 for the last digit, divide, repeat, then reverse (or insert at
the front). 0 needs its own case, or the loop never runs and you return
"". Decoding is Horner's rule: value = value * 62 + digit, left to right.
Why 62? Those are the characters that are safe in a URL path without
escaping. bit.ly, TinyURL and every "design a URL shortener" interview
answer use it; capacity() is the back-of-envelope step that tells you 7
characters cover 3.5 trillion links, so a 64-bit counter never runs out
before the code length has to grow.
The classic bug is silent overflow in decode. A long wraps around on
overflow, so "aZl8N0y58M8" (one past Long.MAX_VALUE) would decode to a
large negative id and fetch someone else's link, or crash later far
from the cause. Math.multiplyExact/addExact throw ArithmeticException
on overflow; translating that into IllegalArgumentException keeps the
error at the boundary where the bad input arrived.
indexOf(ch) == -1 rejects foreign characters; it also makes the decode
case-sensitive for free, because 'a' and 'A' are different digits.
Note what base62 does NOT give you: sequential ids produce guessable
sequential codes. Real shorteners shuffle ids first (see the README).

javabootcamp/11-partitioning-and-ids/03-.instructions:
**Concepts:** range partitioning · binary search · range scans · splits  
**Level:** ★★☆ core

Bigtable, HBase and CockroachDB keep keys in sorted ranges. Finish the
nested class RangePartitioner: split points ["g", "p"] make partition
0 = everything below "g", 1 = ["g", "p"), 2 = "p" and above (a split
point starts its partition). The constructor copies the points and
throws IllegalArgumentException unless they are strictly ascending.
partitionOf(key) finds a key's partition. partitionsFor(from, to) lists,
ascending, the partitions a scan of [from, to) touches (to excluded;
from == to is an empty scan → []; from > to → IllegalArgumentException).
split(at) adds a split point to relieve a hot partition (an existing
point → IllegalArgumentException); splitPoints() is a read-only view
and count() is the number of partitions (split points + 1).
Static evenSplits(sortedSample, n) picks n - 1 split points from a
sorted key sample: the elements at index i * size / n for i = 1..n-1
(n < 1 → IllegalArgumentException).

    partitionOf("kiwi") → 1     partitionOf("p") → 2
    partitionsFor("f", "h") → [0, 1]    partitionsFor("a", "g") → [0]
    evenSplits([a, b, c, d, e, f, g, h], 4) → [c, e, g]

hint: the partition of a key is how many split points are <= it.
javabootcamp/11-partitioning-and-ids/03-.explanation:
Range partitioning keeps neighbouring keys together, which buys the one
thing hash partitioning cannot: a range scan ("all orders for customer
42", "events between 10:00 and 11:00") touches only the partitions that
overlap it. The price is hot spots: sequential keys (timestamps, auto
ids) all land in the last partition. Systems answer with split(): when
a range grows hot or large, cut it in two and move one half.
The partition of a key = the number of split points <= key, which is a
binary search. Collections.binarySearch returns -(insertion point) - 1
for a missing key; for a key equal to a split point it returns its
index, and the key belongs to the partition AFTER it (index + 1),
because a split point starts its range. Getting that boundary wrong is
the classic bug, and the tests pin both sides of it.
partitionsFor uses the same function on both ends, and the exclusive
end matters: a scan of [a, g) must not touch partition 1 just because
"g" is where partition 1 starts. So the scan ends in partitionOf(to),
minus one when `to` is exactly a split point (then no key of that
partition is below `to`).
evenSplits is how operators pre-split a table: sample the keys, take
evenly spaced quantiles, and every partition starts with the same load.

javabootcamp/11-partitioning-and-ids/04-.instructions:
**Concepts:** consistent hashing · virtual nodes · TreeMap · ceilingEntry  
**Level:** ★★☆ core

Dynamo, Cassandra and many cache clients place nodes on a hash ring.
Finish the nested class Ring(vnodes, hash): addNode(name) puts vnodes
points on the ring, at hash(name + "#" + i) for i = 0..vnodes-1, and
nodeFor(key) walks clockwise from hash(key): the owner is the node of
the first point >= hash(key) (a point equal to it counts), wrapping to
the lowest point when hash(key) is past the last one. Hashes compare as
plain signed longs. removeNode(name) takes all its points off.
nodes() lists node names in sorted order. Adding a node twice or
removing an unknown one → IllegalArgumentException, vnodes < 1 →
IllegalArgumentException, nodeFor on an empty ring →
IllegalStateException. Use the given hash64 for real keys.

    points A#0=100, B#0=200, C#0=300
    nodeFor(key hashing to 150)   → "B"
    nodeFor(key hashing to 200)   → "B"      (on the point)
    nodeFor(key hashing to 301)   → "A"      (wraps around)
    after removeNode("B"): 150    → "C"

hint: TreeMap.ceilingEntry(h), then firstEntry() when it returns null.
javabootcamp/11-partitioning-and-ids/04-.explanation:
With hash mod N, changing N reshuffles almost every key (exercise 01).
A ring fixes that: nodes and keys live on the same circle of hash
values and a key belongs to the next node clockwise. Adding a node only
claims the arc just before its points; removing one hands its arcs to
the next points along. Only about 1/N of the keys move, and every key
that moves goes to (or comes from) the node that changed.
A TreeMap<Long, String> IS the ring: ceilingEntry(h) is "first point
>= h", and a null answer means we fell off the end, so wrap with
firstEntry(). Two bugs are common: using higherEntry (a key exactly on
a point then skips its owner), and forgetting the wrap (keys past the
last point get null or an exception).
Virtual nodes: one point per node gives wildly uneven arcs; one node
can own half the circle. Giving every node many points (100-256 is
typical) averages the arc lengths out, so each node owns close to 1/N
of the keys, and when a node leaves, its load spreads over all the
others instead of landing on one neighbour.
removeNode deletes exactly the points addNode created, so the same
"name#i" formula must be used both ways. The hash is injected (a
ToLongFunction) so tests can place points exactly; hash64 is FNV-1a
followed by a 64-bit mixer, so similar names still spread out.

javabootcamp/11-partitioning-and-ids/05-.instructions:
**Concepts:** highest random weight · replica placement · comparators  
**Level:** ★★☆ core

Rendezvous (highest-random-weight) hashing needs no ring: every node
scores every key and the highest score wins. A node's score for a key
is hash.applyAsLong(node + "|" + key), compared as a plain signed long;
an equal score goes to the alphabetically smaller node name. Write
owner(key, nodes, hash), and replicas(key, nodes, n, hash): the n
best-scoring nodes, best first (all nodes when n exceeds their count).
Both ignore the order of `nodes`. No nodes, or n < 1 →
IllegalArgumentException. Use the given hash64 for real keys.

    scores for "k": A|k=10, B|k=30, C|k=20
    owner("k", [A, B, C], h)          → "B"
    replicas("k", [C, A, B], 2, h)    → [B, C]
    replicas("k", [A, B, C], 9, h)    → [B, C, A]

hint: one Comparator (score descending, then name) serves both methods.
javabootcamp/11-partitioning-and-ids/05-.explanation:
Rendezvous hashing (Thaler & Ravishankar, 1996) gets the same "only
1/N of the keys move" property as a ring with far less machinery: no
sorted structure, no virtual nodes. Each node's score for a key is an
independent pseudo-random number, so each node wins about 1/N of the
keys. Remove a node and only the keys it was winning need a new owner
(their runner-up); every other key's winner still has the highest
score. Add a node and it only steals the keys where it now scores
highest. The cost is O(N) hashing per lookup, which is nothing for the
tens of nodes most clusters have.
replicas() is where it shines: sorting all nodes by score gives a
per-key preference list. Take the top 3 and you have replica placement
that stays stable as nodes come and go; when the primary dies, the
next node in the list is already a replica. Apache Ignite's default
affinity function places partitions exactly this way.
The comparator must be TOTAL. Comparing scores alone lets two nodes
with equal scores come out in input order, so two servers holding the
node list in different orders would disagree about the owner, which is
exactly what a placement function must never do. Breaking ties on the
name makes the answer a function of the set, not the list. Use
Long.compare (not subtraction, which overflows on large hashes), and
reverse only the score part.

javabootcamp/11-partitioning-and-ids/06-.instructions:
**Concepts:** distributed ids · bit packing · shifts and masks · clocks  
**Level:** ★★☆ core

Twitter's Snowflake hands out unique, time-ordered 64-bit ids with no
coordination. Finish the nested class Snowflake(epochMs, worker, clock):
an id is (now - epochMs) << 22 | worker << 12 | sequence, with worker
in 0..1023 (else IllegalArgumentException) and sequence in 0..4095.
next() reads the clock exactly once. A new millisecond starts the
sequence at 0; the same millisecond as the previous id adds 1. When the
sequence would pass 4095, keep reading the clock until it moves past
that millisecond, then use sequence 0 there. A clock that moved back
behind the previous id's millisecond → IllegalStateException. Static
parse(id, epochMs) splits an id into Parts (timestamp in absolute ms).

    epoch 0, worker 7, clock 5:   next() → (5 << 22) | (7 << 12) | 0
    same millisecond again:       next() → ... | 1
    parse(that id, 0)             → Parts[timestampMs=5, worker=7,
                                          sequence=1]

hint: mask with 0x3FF (10 bits) and 0xFFF (12 bits) after shifting.
javabootcamp/11-partitioning-and-ids/06-.explanation:
A database sequence is one machine everyone must ask. Snowflake moves
id generation into every process: 41 bits of milliseconds (about 69
years from a custom epoch), 10 bits of worker id (assigned once per
process, so two workers never collide), and 12 bits of sequence for up
to 4096 ids per worker per millisecond. Because time is in the high
bits, ids sort by creation time, which keeps B-tree inserts appending
at the right edge instead of splitting pages all over the index.
The sequence rules are the heart of it. Same millisecond: count up. New
millisecond: reset to 0. Ran out (the 4097th id in one ms): you must
NOT wrap to 0 in the same ms (a duplicate) and must NOT let 4096 spill
into the worker bits (a different worker's id). Snowflake waits for the
next millisecond; with an injected clock that is a loop that keeps
reading it. Reading the clock exactly once per normal call is part of
the contract so tests can script time.
Clocks do move backwards (NTP corrections, VM migration). Issuing ids
then could repeat ones already handed out, so refuse loudly; real
deployments alert on it or wait out the gap.
parse is the reverse: >>> 22 for the time (unsigned shift, though ids
stay positive for 69 years), then (id >>> 12) & 0x3FF and id & 0xFFF.
The clock is a LongSupplier, never System.currentTimeMillis(), so the
tests are deterministic.

javabootcamp/11-partitioning-and-ids/07-.instructions:
**Concepts:** probabilistic sets · double hashing · BitSet · false positives  
**Level:** ★★★ stretch

Cassandra and LevelDB check a Bloom filter before reading a file from
disk. Finish the nested class Bloom(bits, hashes) (either < 1 →
IllegalArgumentException). With h = hash64(key), h1 = (int) h and
h2 = (int) (h >>> 32), positions(key) is, for i = 0..hashes-1,
Math.floorMod(h1 + i * h2, bits) computed in int arithmetic (overflow
wraps). add(key) sets those bits; mightContain(key) is true only if all
are set; bitsSet() counts set bits. Static optimalHashes(bits, items) =
Math.round(bits / items * ln 2) as a double division, at least 1
(items < 1 → IllegalArgumentException). Static falsePositiveRate(bits,
hashes, items) = (1 - e^(-hashes * items / bits)) ^ hashes.

    var f = new Bloom(1000, 4);  f.add("apple");
    f.mightContain("apple")           → true   (always, once added)
    f.mightContain("banana")          → false  (almost always)
    optimalHashes(10_000, 1_000)      → 7
    falsePositiveRate(10_000, 7, 1_000) → about 0.0082

hint: two hashes are enough; Kirsch and Mitzenmacher showed why.
javabootcamp/11-partitioning-and-ids/07-.explanation:
A Bloom filter answers "definitely not here" or "maybe here" using a
few bits per key. An LSM storage engine keeps one per SSTable: a read
for a missing key skips every file whose filter says no, which is most
of them. A "maybe" costs one real lookup; a "no" is always right,
because adding a key sets all of its bits and bits are never cleared.
That is also why a plain Bloom filter cannot delete.
k independent hash functions are expensive; double hashing derives
them from one 64-bit hash: g_i = h1 + i * h2. Kirsch and Mitzenmacher
proved this keeps the same false-positive rate. The traps are Java's:
h1 + i * h2 overflows int (fine, it is meant to wrap) and can be
negative, so the index needs Math.floorMod; Math.abs would give
different positions (and a negative one for MIN_VALUE). And i must
start at 0, so the first position is h1 itself.
The formulas are the design tool. With m bits, n items and k hashes the
false-positive rate is about (1 - e^(-kn/m))^k, minimised at
k = (m/n) ln 2. At 10 bits per key that is k = 7 and under 1 percent;
the test measures it on 10,000 keys the filter never saw. Integer
division in optimalHashes (10_000 / 1_500 = 6) silently changes k,
so divide as doubles.

javabootcamp/11-partitioning-and-ids/08-.instructions:
**Concepts:** replication · R + W > N · versions · read repair  
**Level:** ★★★ stretch

Dynamo-style stores keep N copies and let you pick R and W. Finish the
nested class Cluster(n, r, w) (unless 1 <= r <= n and 1 <= w <= n →
IllegalArgumentException); replicas are numbered 0..n-1. Static
isStrong(n, r, w) is r + w > n. write(key, value, reachable): fewer
than w reachable → IllegalStateException, nothing stored and no
version used; otherwise the next version (1, 2, 3... cluster-wide) is
stored on EVERY reachable replica and returned. read(key, reachable):
fewer than r reachable → IllegalStateException; otherwise contact only
the r LOWEST-numbered reachable replicas and return the value with the
highest version among them (Optional.empty() if none has the key),
then read repair: copy that newest Versioned onto each contacted
replica that is missing it or older. A reachable index outside 0..n-1 →
IllegalArgumentException. stored(replica, key) peeks at one replica.

    N=3 R=1 W=1:  write("x","a",{0,1,2}), write("x","b",{0})
    read("x", {1, 2})        → "a"     (stale: R + W <= N)
    N=3 R=2 W=2:  any read overlaps the last write → "b"

hint: the newest version wins, wherever it was found.
javabootcamp/11-partitioning-and-ids/08-.explanation:
With N copies, a write that waits for W acknowledgements and a read
that asks R replicas are guaranteed to overlap in at least one replica
when R + W > N (pigeonhole: the two sets have R + W members among N
slots). That one shared replica holds the latest version, and taking
the highest version among the replies finds it. Cassandra's QUORUM
(R = W = majority) and Dynamo's tunable N/R/W are this inequality.
Choose R + W <= N (say R = W = 1) and you get lower latency and higher
availability, but a read can miss the last write entirely. The tests
make that visible by having reads contact the lowest-numbered reachable
replicas, so the stale case is deterministic instead of unlucky.
Versions, not arrival order, decide what is newest: a replica list is
not a timeline. Real systems use timestamps or vector clocks (module
13); a cluster-wide counter is the simplest stand-in.
Two failure rules matter. A write that cannot reach W replicas must
fail BEFORE storing anything here (real systems may leave partial
writes behind, which is why reads must tolerate them). And a read that
cannot reach R replicas fails rather than quietly returning less.
Read repair is how replicas converge without a background job: the
read already knows which contacted replicas are behind, so it writes
the newest version back to them. Only contacted replicas are repaired.
